title: Delhi Dust Hotspots Resist Cleanup as Winter Plan Targets Roads and Construction
excerpt: Delhi's worst air concentrates where dust and traffic regenerate it daily. The winter plan answers with 854 swept roads, AI-watched construction sites, IIT Delhi source tracking and a 40-site technology pilot.
body:
• Delhi's pollution hotspots persist because their sources are local and continuous: road dust from unpaved surfaces, construction activity, idling traffic and waste burning regenerate particulate matter daily.
  • The Winter Action Plan runs November 1, 2026 to February 28, 2027, with a 'No PUC, No Fuel' rule, a bar on non-BS-VI vehicles registered outside Delhi, and AI cameras monitoring construction sites.
  • Mechanised sweeping will expand to 854 roads across 250 wards, including about 609 km of narrower roads, and 30 new electric sweepers have been cleared for neighbourhood streets.
  • A separate Rs 104-crore pilot will test pollution-cutting technology at 40 sites with a target of cutting PM10 and PM2.5 by 20% at each site over a one-year trial monitored by the DPCC.

Delhi is again preparing for its winter pollution season with a familiar problem: the city's worst air is not evenly spread. It concentrates in hotspots — transport hubs, industrial pockets and congested corridors — where dust and emissions are produced every day, close to where people live and work. The Times of India's examination of the city's war on dust asks why those hotspots remain a challenge despite years of action plans, and the measures announced this month show both the scale of the response and why it has struggled to hold.

Why hotspots do not clear

A hotspot is a source problem, not just a weather problem. Previous Delhi Pollution Control Committee assessments identified road dust from unpaved roads and vehicle tailpipe emissions as the key concerns on stretches such as Chandni Chowk's main market road, Lotus Temple Road and Baba Kharak Singh Marg. At Anand Vihar, officials selected the bus terminal area because of heavy vehicle parking and congestion. Where unpaved surfaces keep generating dust and vehicles keep idling in traffic, a one-time cleanup is undone within days — the intervention operates against a continuing source.

Geography compounds it. Several of the city's most polluted outer and industrial areas — Bawana and Narela in north Delhi, Mayapuri in the west and the Okhla Industrial Area in the southeast — were not included in the government's new 40-site technology pilot, which concentrates on commercial areas. Central and South Delhi account for 19 of the 40 sites, and commercial locations make up 29 of them, including Khan Market, Connaught Place and the bus terminals at Kashmere Gate, Anand Vihar and Sarai Kale Khan.

The winter plan, in specifics

The government's Winter Action Plan, led by Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, runs from November 1, 2026 to February 28, 2027. Its transport measures include enforcing 'No PUC, No Fuel' — vehicles without a valid Pollution Under Control certificate will not be sold fuel at designated pumps — and restricting entry for vehicles registered outside Delhi that do not meet BS-VI emission standards. The plan also proposes encouraging 50 per cent work from home to cut commuting, and expanding electric buses, Metro use and last-mile connectivity.

On dust specifically, construction and demolition sites will be watched by artificial intelligence-enabled cameras linked to the government's central control and command centre, and the DPCC has stepped up site inspections and issued show-cause notices where violations were found. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi and the Urban Development Secretary conducted a joint inspection of hotspots and construction sites in the South Zone on October 11.

Sweepers and source tracking

Two cabinet decisions target road dust directly. Mechanised sweeping will be expanded to roads where it is currently unavailable — about 609 kilometres of roads with a right of way under 10 metres, covering 854 roads across 250 municipal wards. Separately, as Nation Press reported, 30 electric mechanical sweepers have been cleared for the smaller arterial and residential roads that larger machines cannot enter. The electric specification matters: diesel sweepers would add emissions while removing dust.

The cabinet also approved a five-year collaboration with IIT Delhi to monitor and analyse the sources of PM2.5 and PM10 continuously, tracking how much vehicles, road dust and biomass burning each contribute through the day. That source attribution is the missing link in hotspot policy: enforcement can target the specific source at a specific location instead of applying blanket restrictions across the city.

A measured experiment

The Rs 104-crore pilot takes the same targeted approach. Firms will install certified technology — outdoor purifiers, mist-based scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators are among the options — at 40 public and commercial sites, with four weeks to install and commission after handover. Each site must cut PM10 and PM2.5 by 20 per cent and maintain that reduction through a one-year trial, with daily DPCC-supervised monitoring and assessment by an independent committee. Equipment must be certified by a government laboratory and must not create secondary hazards such as ozone or excess noise, according to the plan's published details.

What to watch

The test this winter is execution, not announcement. The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) still governs emergency restrictions when air quality deteriorates, and Stage 1 was invoked on October 21 as the Air Quality Index entered the 'poor' category. Whether hotspots improve will depend on the unglamorous chain behind the headlines: paved and maintained road surfaces, working sweepers on schedule, construction sites actually complying between inspections, and IIT Delhi's source data reaching enforcement teams fast enough to act on. Delhi has named the machines, the roads and the target pollutants this time. The hotspot readings through November and December will show whether that specificity translates into cleaner air where it is worst.
